source_text: Licuit et Valentino ex privilegio haeretico carnem Christi spiritalem comminisci. Quidvis eam fingere potuit quisquis humanam credere noluit, quando, quod ad omnes dictum est, si humana non fuit nec ex homine, non video ex qua substantia ipse se Christus hominem et filium hominis pronuntiarit: Nunc autem vultis occidere hominem, veritatem ad vos locutum, et: Dominus est sabbati filius hominis. De ipso enim Essias: Homo in plaga, et sciens ferre imbecillitatem. Et Hieremias: Et homo est, et quis cognovit illum? Et Daniel: Et super nubes tanquam filius hominis. Etiam Paulus apostolus: Mediator dei et hominum homo Christus Iesus. Item Petrus in Actis Apostolorum: Iesum Nazarenum virum vobis a deo destinatum, utique hominem. Haec sola sufficere vice praescriptionis debuerunt ad testimonium carnis humanae et ex homine sumptae et non spiritalis, sicut nec animalis nec sidereae nec imaginariae, si sine studio et artifieio contentionis haereses esse potuissent. Nam ut penes quendam ex Valentini factiuncula legi, primo non putant terrenam et humanam Christo substantiam informatam, ne deterior angelis dominus deprehendatur, qui non terrenae carnis extiterunt, dehinc quod oporteret similem nostri carnem similiter nasci, non de spiritu, nec de deo, sed ex viri voluntate. Et cur non de corruptela, sed de incorruptela? Et quare non, sicut et illa resurrexit et in caelo resumpta est, ita et nostra par eius statim adsumitur? Aut cur illa par nostrae non aeque in terram dissoluta est? Talia et ethnici volutabant. Ergo dei filius in tantum humilitatis exhaustus? et, Si resurrexit in exemplum spei nostrae, cur nihil tale de nobis probatum est? Merito ethnici talia; sed merito et haeretici. Numquid enim inter illos distat, nisi quod ethnici non credendo credunt, at haeretici credendo non credunt? Legunt denique: Minorasti eum modico citra angelos, et negant inferiorem substantiam Christi, nec hominem se, sed vermem pronuntiantis, qui nec formam habuit nec speciem; sed forma eius ignobilis, despecta citra omnes homines, homo in plaga, et sciens ferre imbecillitatem. Agnoscunt hominem deo mixtum, et negant hominem. Mortuum credunt, et quod est mortuum ex incorruptela natum esse contendunt, quasi corruptela aliud sit a morte. Sed et nostra caro statim resurgere debebat. Exspecta. Nondum inimicos suos Christus oppressit, ut eum amicis de inimicis triumphet.
thought_title: The heretics' privilege of inventing Christ's flesh
orientation: Tertullian is refuting the heretical views of Christ's flesh, now turning to Valentinus, who claimed Christ's flesh was spiritual.
pass_a_gloss: It was permitted also to Valentinus, by the privilege of heretics, to invent a spiritual flesh of Christ. Anyone who was unwilling to believe it human could fashion it as anything he wished, since, as has been said to all, if it was not human nor from man, I do not see from what substance Christ himself declared himself man and Son of Man: 'But now you wish to kill a man, who has spoken truth to you,' and: 'The Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.' For about him Isaiah says: 'A man in affliction, and knowing how to bear weakness.' And Jeremiah: 'And he is a man, and who has known him?' And Daniel: 'And upon the clouds as a Son of Man.' Also Paul the apostle: 'Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus.' Likewise Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: 'Jesus of Nazareth, a man destined for you by God,' certainly a man. These things alone ought to have sufficed in place of a prescription as testimony of flesh that is human and taken from man and not spiritual, just as not made of soul nor starry nor imaginary, if heresies could have existed without zeal and artifice of contention. For as I read in a certain one of Valentinus's little faction, first they do not think that an earthly and human substance was formed for Christ, lest the Lord be found inferior to the angels, who did not exist from earthly flesh; then that it was fitting that a flesh like ours be born in like manner, not from spirit, nor from God, but from the will of a man. And why not from corruption, but from incorruption? And why, just as that flesh rose again and was taken up into heaven, is not our flesh, equal to it, taken up immediately? Or why was that flesh, equal to ours, not likewise dissolved into the earth? Such things even the heathen were turning over. Therefore was the Son of God emptied to such a degree of humility? And, if he rose again as an example of our hope, why has nothing of the kind been proven about us? Rightly do the heathen think such things; but rightly also the heretics. For is there any difference between them, except that the heathen by not believing believe, but the heretics by believing do not believe? Finally they read: 'You made him a little lower than the angels,' and they deny the inferior substance of Christ, who declared himself not a man but a worm, who had neither form nor beauty; but his form was ignoble, despised beyond all men, a man in affliction, and knowing how to bear weakness. They acknowledge a man mixed with God, and they deny the man. They believe him dead, and they contend that what is dead was born from incorruption, as if corruption were something other than death. But our flesh also ought to have risen immediately. Wait. Christ has not yet crushed his enemies, so that he may triumph over them for his friends from his enemies.

choices.why: Keeps the paradox of the heretical claim; 'spiritual' is the glossary term for spiritalis, and 'flesh' for caro.
Preserves the ironic tone; 'privilege' captures the license Tertullian says heretics claim.
Legal term kept to show Tertullian's forensic method; 'prescription' is the technical term for a preliminary objection.
Diminutive conveys Tertullian's contempt for the Valentinian splinter group.

choices.english: emptied to such a degree of humility
choices.why: Echoes Philippians 2:7 language of emptying; 'emptied' keeps the kenosis allusion.
Standard rendering for Tertullian's term for pagans; keeps the contrast with heretics.

pass_b_english: Valentinus too enjoyed the heretic's privilege of inventing a spiritual flesh for Christ. Anyone who refused to believe that flesh was human could make it into whatever he pleased. For if it was not human and not from a human being—and this applies to all of them—I do not see from what substance Christ could have declared himself to be a man and the Son of Man: “But now you are trying to kill a man who has told you the truth” (John 8:40), and “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath” (Matthew 12:8). Isaiah says of him: “A man of suffering, and knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah 53:3). And Jeremiah: “He is a man, and who has known him?” (Jeremiah 17:9). And Daniel: “And on the clouds, like a Son of Man” (Daniel 7:13). The apostle Paul too: “The mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Likewise Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: “Jesus of Nazareth, a man sent to you by God” (Acts 2:22)—certainly a man.

These alone should have been enough, in place of a formal objection, to testify that his flesh was human, taken from a human being, and not spiritual—just as it was not made of soul, nor starry, nor imaginary—if heresies could exist without the zeal and cunning of contention. For instance, as I have read in the work of someone from Valentinus's little faction, they first do not hold that an earthly and human substance was formed for Christ, lest the Lord be found inferior to the angels, who were not made of earthly flesh. Then they say that a flesh like ours ought to be born in the same way—not from the Spirit, nor from God, but from a man's will.

And why not from corruption, but from incorruption? And why is our flesh, equal to his, not immediately taken up, just as his rose and was taken up into heaven? Or why was his flesh, equal to ours, not likewise dissolved into the earth? The heathen used to ponder such things. “So the Son of God was emptied to such a degree of humility?” And: “If he rose as an example for our hope, why has nothing of the kind been proven for us?” The heathen are right to say such things—but so are the heretics. Is there any difference between them, except that the heathen believe by not believing, while the heretics do not believe by believing?

They read, after all: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8:5), and they deny the inferior substance of Christ—the one who declared himself not a man but a worm, who had neither form nor beauty; but his form was ignoble, despised beyond all men, a man of suffering, and knowing how to bear weakness (Isaiah 53:2-3). They acknowledge a man mixed with God, and they deny the man. They believe he died, and they contend that what died was born from incorruption—as if corruption were anything other than death.
But our flesh too should have risen immediately. Wait. Christ has not yet crushed his enemies, so that he may triumph over them with his friends.

problems.source_quote: Et Hieremias: Et homo est, et quis cognovit illum?
problems.why: The Latin quotation is not from Jeremiah 17:9; the verse cited does not contain that wording.
problems.fix: And Jeremiah: “He is a man, and who has known him?” (correct Jeremiah reference, e.g., Jeremiah 9:22) or remove the incorrect citation.
problems.ruling: Jeremiah 17:9 is 'prava est cor'; 'Et homo est et quis cognovit illum' is from Jeremiah 17:9 LXX, not the cited verse.

problems.quote: they first refuse to believe that an earthly and human substance was formed for Christ

problems.ruling: Latin 'non putant' = they do not think, not 'refuse to believe' which adds volitional denial absent in source.

problems.quote: And why, just as his flesh rose and was taken up into heaven, is our flesh, equal to his, taken up immediately?
problems.source_quote: Et quare non, sicut et illa resurrexit et in caelo resumpta est, ita et nostra par eius statim adsumitur?
problems.why: Source has 'quare non' = 'why is our flesh NOT taken up'; English drops the negation, flipping the meaning.
problems.fix: And why is our flesh, equal to his, not immediately taken up, just as his rose and was taken up into heaven?
problems.ruling: Latin 'quare non' = why not, asks why our flesh is NOT taken up; English drops negation, reversing meaning.

problems.quote: so that he may triumph over them with his friends, from among his enemies.
problems.source_quote: ut eum amicis de inimicis triumphet.
problems.why: English adds "from among his enemies" which is not present in the Latin.
problems.fix: so that he may triumph over them with his friends.
problems.ruling: Latin 'de inimicis' means 'over enemies'; 'from among enemies' mistranslates the preposition, misleading the reader.

last_rejected.why: Source means 'from a man's will' but context is Christ's birth; 'viri' = 'a man' not 'the man', and this is the heretics' argument that flesh like ours should be born from a human father's will, i.e., sexual generation.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'ex viri voluntate' = 'by/from a man's will'; English 'from a man's will' conveys same meaning

last_rejected.quote: who declared himself not a man but a worm, who had neither form nor beauty; but his form was ignoble, despised beyond all men, a man of suffering, and knowing how to bear weakness (Isaiah 53:2-3)
last_rejected.source_quote: nec hominem se, sed vermem pronuntiantis, qui nec formam habuit nec speciem
last_rejected.why: The worm who is not a man is Psalm 22:6. Isaiah 53:2-3 is only the form, suffering, and weakness.
last_rejected.fix: who called himself not a man but a worm (Psalm 22:6), who had neither form nor beauty; his form was mean, despised below all men, a man of suffering, knowing how to bear weakness (Isaiah 53:2-3).
last_rejected.ruling: Source's own scripture is not cited; 'vermem... qui nec formam habuit' blends Ps 22:6 with Isaiah 53:2-3. Citation Isaiah 53:2-3 covers the form/suffering clauses; worm clause lacks a reference, a minor omission, not a mistranslation.
